extracted.intended_audience: people learning to use TeX/plain-TeX (beginners to intermediate users who write/manipulate TeX source files)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for preparing, diagnosing, and correcting TeX manuscripts: detecting and interpreting overfull/underfull boxes and error messages, controlling spacing and tolerance, managing interaction modes, and understanding tokenization/category codes and character handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting overfull/underfull box messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Each overfull (or underfull) box message reports the location in the input (paragraph lines), an abbreviated view of the box contents, the font used, and how much the copy sticks out (e.g., 'Overfull \hbox (0.98807pt too wide) in paragraph at lines 7--11').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the transcript/log file (story.log) to see these messages; use the abbreviated contents to identify the offending text (the log shows hyphenations tried). The '[]' in messages can indicate paragraph indentation or complex constructions (e.g., an umlaut). Use the reported amount that the box sticks out to judge remedies (rewriting, hyphenation hints, or changing tolerance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hyphenation hints to cure narrow-column overfull boxes
rubrics_metrics.description: When TeX reports an overfull box and hyphenation points exist that could help, you can give TeX explicit hyphenation information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two methods: insert discretionary hyphens inline (e.g., 'gal\-axy') each time, or declare them once with a \hyphenation{gal-axy} in the preamble. Examine log to see which hyphens TeX tried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting \tolerance to allow wider spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX uses a numerical parameter 'tolerance' to determine acceptable line spacing; increasing \tolerance permits lines with wider inter-word spaces rather than producing overfull boxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \hsize=2in \tolerance=1600 \input story removed overfull boxes for 2-inch columns. \tolerance=10000 is treated as infinite (will never produce overfull boxes except when an unhyphenatable word exceeds the column width). Choose tolerance appropriate to column width or rewrite the copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding and using 'badness' values
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX assigns a numerical 'badness' to each line to assess spacing quality (0 perfect; higher numbers indicate more loose/tight spacing). Plain TeX normally stipulates that no line's badness should exceed 200.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Badness values are font-dependent. Example descriptors given: 0 perfect, 12 somewhat tight, 100 somewhat tight, 200 loose, 1000 bad, 5000 awful. Use badness together with \tolerance and \hbadness to control warnings and behavior; for very narrow columns, allow higher tolerances or rewrite text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using \hbadness to control underfull-box warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: A threshold parameter \hbadness determines when TeX reports underfull boxes (lines whose badness exceeds \hbadness). Plain TeX sets \hbadness=1000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set \hbadness to a lower value (e.g., 500) to be warned about underfull boxes you care about, or raise it to suppress warnings. Combine with \tolerance to choose whether you prefer overfull boxes (inspectable) or underfull warnings (informational).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \hfuzz to ignore slight overfull boxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The \hfuzz parameter allows TeX to ignore boxes that are only slightly overfull; e.g., \hfuzz=1pt ignores boxes that stick out by 1pt or less. Plain TeX defaults to \hfuzz=0.1pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set \hfuzz to suppress trivial overfull box messages when you deem small protrusions acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to prefer inspection of overfull boxes vs. automated tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Two strategies: set high \tolerance and adjust \hbadness to avoid overfull boxes but get underfull warnings (if you just want to know how bad spacing is), or set \tolerance equal to a desired maximum badness so TeX might produce overfull boxes you can inspect and correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have time to fix spacing, the second option is better (overfull boxes show exactly how much protrudes); if you only need a quick assessment, the first option is faster though it may use more compute time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \raggedright to avoid forcing right-justified spacing in very narrow columns
rubrics_metrics.description: \raggedright tells TeX not to justify the right margin, so badness then reflects extra space at the right margin rather than inter-word spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When columns are very narrow, \raggedright can produce more reasonable output; after specifying \raggedright, test to see the badness assigned to lines (Exercise 6.5 suggests experimenting to determine per-line badness under ragged-right).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design macros to allow flexible spacing around punctuation (e.g., dashes) in narrow columns
rubrics_metrics.description: In narrow columns it may be better to allow white space before/after a dash when other spaces in the same line are being stretched; redefine dash spacing accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define a macro (e.g., \dash) that permits flexible spacing around the dash so lines can stretch more naturally; Exercise 6.6 suggests implementing such a macro.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting TeX error messages and using the interaction menu
rubrics_metrics.description: When TeX stops with an error it prints '!' and two lines of context (what it read and what is next) and a '?' prompt. Typing '?' at the prompt shows the list of available responses (Return, S, R, Q, I, E, numbers, H, X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common responses: Return (resume), S (scroll future errors), R (run without stopping), Q (quiet run), I (insert text), E (edit file), number (delete next tokens), H (help — gives informal message and suggestions), X (exit). Use 'H' for unfamiliar errors and 'E' to fix files; inserted text does not change the source file. Chapter 27 and Appendix B have more on recovery strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control interaction modes from the source with \scrollmode, \nonstopmode, \batchmode, \errorstopmode
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX primitives correspond to online responses: \scrollmode ~ 'S', \nonstopmode ~ 'R', \batchmode ~ 'Q'; \errorstopmode returns to normal interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place these commands in your file to control how TeX behaves on errors (changes are global even inside groups). Some installations may revert to \errorstopmode on interrupts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding multiline macro-context error messages and where to look for clues
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiline error messages show several two-line pairs of context representing nested macro expansions; the top line of a pair shows what TeX just read (triggering the error) and the bottom line shows what it was about to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multiline errors the most useful clues are usually the bottom line (what you typed) and the top line (what triggered the error). Use \errorcontextlines to increase/decrease the amount of context shown when diagnosing complex format-package errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control amount of macro-context shown in errors with \errorcontextlines
rubrics_metrics.description: \errorcontextlines sets how many additional two-line context items TeX prints in error messages (Plain TeX sets \errorcontextlines=5). Setting it to 0 shows only the top and bottom pairs; setting it high (e.g., 100) will reveal much more context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using format packages with deep expansion, reduce context to avoid overwhelming output (or increase it when you need more detail); omitted parts are indicated by '...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tokenization rules: how TeX converts input to tokens
rubrics_metrics.description: When TeX reads a line it converts text into tokens: either a character with an attached category code (one of 16 categories) or a control sequence. A token stream (the 'stomach') is what TeX digests to typeset; input-line rules (e.g., a return is like a space, two spaces count as one, blank line ends paragraph) apply during tokenization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that control sequences become single tokens (indivisible during digestion), spaces after control words are ignored during tokenization, and category codes are attached to character tokens at read time (and remain fixed for those tokens even if catcodes change later).

rubrics_metrics.name: The 16 category codes and reserved special characters in plain TeX
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 16 character categories (0..15) such as escape (0), begin-group (1), end-group (2), math shift (3), alignment tab (4), end-of-line (5), parameter (6), superscript (7), subscript (8), ignored (9), space (10), letter (11), other (12), active (13), comment (14), invalid (15). In plain TeX the characters \ { } $ & # ^ _ % ~ are reserved and cannot be used normally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need one of those symbols in text, use their escaping control sequences (e.g., \$, \%, \&, \#, \_) or use control sequences that produce them. Use \catcode to change categories if necessary, but be careful because earlier token lists retain their original category attachments (locality rules apply).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence of category codes in already-created token lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a character token is created with a given category code, that attachment is permanent for that token; changing \catcode later affects only subsequently read characters and token lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful when changing \catcode inside groups — tokens already in buffers/expandable constructs keep their old meanings. Use \catcode early if needed for format creation; INITEX and format files typically set up category codes initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of \string, \csname...\endcsname, \number, \romannumeral, \uppercase and \lowercase
rubrics_metrics.description: \string converts a control sequence into the list of characters of its name (each produced as category 12 'other' tokens); \csname...\endcsname constructs a control sequence from a sequence of character tokens; \number and \romannumeral produce decimal or lowercase-roman textual tokens; \uppercase and \lowercase convert character tokens using \uccode and \lccode tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \string\TeX yields the characters '\\TeX' (each as 'other'); \csname TeX\endcsname is essentially \TeX; \number-0015 yields '-15'; \romannumeral24 yields 'xxiv'. \uppercase and \lowercase use the mutable \uccode and \lccode values: only nonzero codes produce conversions. Be aware of expansion order: \string, \number, \romannumeral, \csname are done during expansion en route to tokenization, while \uppercase/\lowercase operate 'in the stomach' on token lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct control-sequence names programmatically and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: You can create control sequence names at run-time with \csname...\endcsname; a newly defined name created this way is initially equivalent to \relax until explicitly defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows tricks like testing for undefined control sequences or dynamically defining commands. Beware: tokens between \csname and \endcsname must expand to characters (not primitives that expand to non-character tokens), otherwise the construction is illegal. Use this to build macros like \ifundefined (Exercise 7.7) or to append numerals in names (Exercise 7.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Access arbitrary font characters with \char<number>
rubrics_metrics.description: To refer to any character code (0..255) in the current font use \char<number> (optionally followed by a space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix C shows ASCII code mapping; plain-format defines \% as \char37. Useful when keyboard lacks a character or the key is reserved; an optional space is ignored after numeric constants like '98'.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX's internal use of ASCII codes and device-independent behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX internally uses ASCII code values (Appendix C) for standard characters regardless of the machine's external encoding (EBCDIC, etc.); input files are converted to TeX's internal code and dvi output uses internal codes, ensuring consistent behavior across systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on TeX's mapping to get consistent character codes; consult Appendix C for code numbers (e.g., space =32, return=13). Character code tables may be shown in octal/hex but TeX's internal code is as specified.
